correctness.rationale: RESULT.md lines 4–28 correctly restrict the five forms to diagonal-coordinate equivalence. The three pairings yield 27 distinct lines after the indicated cubic twist; b_i^7/b_i=2^{m_i}, and a line's two exponents translate by the differences of the corresponding m_i. Picard descent over the finite field and averaging the geometric effective cone give exactly the orbit-sum cone: each sum is itself an effective divisor descended over the base field, and every invariant effective class is a nonnegative combination of such sums. Distinct line orbits have nonnegative mutual intersection, so a negative-square trace cannot be a nonnegative combination of the others or share their rays. In rank three the remaining three traces are H and the six negative traces sum to 6H; in rank one there is just the positive H-ray. The independent exhaustive finite calculation confirms all five rows including ranks, trace-class identities, rational lines, point counts and dual extreme rays. The dual count uses successive half-space intersections of a pointed cone; new rays come from opposite-sign adjacent rays, detected by the minimal common active face. This is independent of the supplied active-minor enumeration. The point count also follows from the order-three action with rational trace (3r-7)/2, giving 50+7(3r-7)/2.
residual_risks: This checks the real cones and rank, not a statement of arithmetic integral generators or equivalence under arbitrary projective changes of coordinates.

value.rationale: The family exhausts the diagonal coefficient-class space over the smallest odd finite field of characteristic different from 3 with nontrivial cube classes. It gives a natural finite test of how descent changes the cones: rank five retains every orbit sum as extremal, whereas rank three has no rational lines, six negative extremal traces, and three orbit sums collapsing to the interior hyperplane ray. The full dual counts resolve exact geometry not supplied by rank or number of line orbits. This is a bounded arithmetic classification, not a general theorem about all cubic surfaces.
